Before proving that an object built by a general recipe (extension, quotient, gluing, deformation, limit) has a required property, verify from the shape of the recipe alone that the property is possible at all. A nontrivial centre rules out ICC; a global fixed point rules out a free action; a nonzero kernel rules out injectivity claimed alongside it; a common invariant subobject rules out simplicity or primitivity; a counting or parity obstruction (Euler, degree-sum, Hall) rules out an incidence structure however its pieces are chosen. BATTERY0.truth: FALSE. n = 171 = 9·19 divides 2^171 + 1 (the solutions begin 3, 9, 27, 81, 171). Any valid counterexample must be one of these non-powers of 3; 171 is the smallest.

BATTERY0.statement: For all positive real numbers a, b, c with abc = 1, we have ab + bc + ca ≥ a + b + c.
BATTERY0.truth: FALSE. a = b = 1/2, c = 4 gives ab+bc+ca = 4.25 < 5 = a+b+c. (The reverse inequality is also false: a = b = 2, c = 1/4.)

BATTERY0.statement: Every group in which x^3 = e for every element x is abelian.
BATTERY0.truth: FALSE. The Heisenberg group of upper unitriangular 3×3 matrices over F_3 has order 27, exponent 3, and is non-abelian.

BATTERY0.statement: If f: R → R is differentiable everywhere and f'(0) > 0, then there is δ > 0 such that f is increasing on (−δ, δ).
BATTERY0.truth: FALSE. f(x) = x + 2x² sin(1/x), f(0) = 0: f'(0) = 1 but f'(x) = 1 + 4x sin(1/x) − 2cos(1/x) is negative at points arbitrarily near 0. Only 'f(x) > f(0) > f(−x) near 0' is true.

BATTERY0.statement: Every simple graph on n ≥ 3 vertices with minimum degree at least (n−1)/2 has a Hamiltonian cycle.
BATTERY0.truth: FALSE. K_{k,k+1} has n = 2k+1, minimum degree k = (n−1)/2, and no Hamiltonian cycle (bipartite, odd order). The path on 3 vertices also works. Dirac's theorem needs n/2.
